concepts.title: Why Chunking Comes Before Embedding
concepts.description: Before a single vector gets computed, real documents have to be broken into pieces -- not as an afterthought, but because embedding models enforce their own token limits and because compressing an entire multi-topic document into one vector blurs together everything it discusses, hurting retrieval even when there is no length limit anywhere in sight.
learningObjectives: Explain why embedding models have a fixed maximum input length, and describe what typically happens -- often silently -- when an input exceeds it.
Distinguish the embedding model's own context window limit from the generation LLM's context window limit, and explain why solving one does not solve the other.
Explain the retrieval-granularity problem: why compressing an entire multi-topic document into a single vector produces mediocre similarity scores for queries about any one of its subtopics.
Predict the consequence of silently truncating a document during embedding, and explain why that failure produces no error and no warning.
Explain why chunking is a deliberate, offline preprocessing decision made once per document, before any embedding call happens at all.

sections.heading: Two Separate Context Windows, Two Separate Problems
sections.body:
It's tempting to assume that once a generation model boasts a context window of 128,000 tokens or more, 'context window limits' are basically a solved problem for a RAG pipeline and chunking only mattered back when models were smaller. That reasoning skips over an entirely separate component with its own, usually much smaller, limit: the **embedding model** used to build the searchable index in the first place. Many widely-used sentence-embedding models cap their input at somewhere between 256 and 512 tokens; even larger hosted embedding APIs typically cap out in the low thousands of tokens -- nowhere near the context window of the generation model that eventually reads whatever gets retrieved. These are two independent limits, enforced by two entirely different models doing two entirely different jobs, and raising (or forgetting about) one tells you nothing about the other.

What actually happens when you hand an encoder more tokens than it accepts depends on the specific library and model, but a distressingly common answer is: it just quietly truncates, keeping only the first N tokens and discarding the rest, with no exception raised and no warning printed anywhere.

```python
def tokenize(text):
    return text.split()

def truncate(tokens, max_tokens):
    return tokens[:max_tokens]

def toy_embed(text, max_tokens=8):
    # Stand-in for a real encoder's internal truncate-then-embed behavior --
    # everything past max_tokens is simply never looked at.
    tokens = tokenize(text)
    truncated = truncate(tokens, max_tokens)
    seed = sum(len(t) for t in truncated)
    return [(seed % 5) / 5, (seed % 7) / 7]

document = (
    "The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent driven "
    "primarily by the new enterprise product line launched in March "
    "which exceeded internal projections"
)

print(len(tokenize(document)))            # 23 -- the real document length
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8))   # only the first 8 tokens are ever seen
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=100)) # the full document, for comparison
```

The truncated call doesn't fail, doesn't warn, and returns something that looks exactly like every other embedding vector the pipeline produces. Whatever the document said about the enterprise product line, internal projections, or anything past word 8 -- in this toy example, and in a great many real embedding libraries running with default settings -- is simply never seen by the model at all.

sections.heading: The Retrieval-Granularity Problem: Length Limits Aren't Even the Real Issue
sections.body:
Suppose, hypothetically, an embedding model had no length limit whatsoever and could happily accept an entire 50-page document as a single input. Chunking would still be necessary, for a reason that has nothing to do with token limits at all: a single fixed-length vector has to represent everything the document talks about, all at once, and averaging together several unrelated subtopics produces a vector that represents each of them only weakly.

Recall how encoders actually produce a document-level vector: pooling -- commonly averaging -- many per-token contextual vectors down into one fixed-length result. If a document discusses billing, security, and onboarding in roughly equal measure, its single pooled vector ends up sitting somewhere in the geometric middle of all three topics -- close to each of them, but not nearly as close to any single one as a vector representing *only* that topic would be:

```python
def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = sum(x * x for x in a) ** 0.5
    nb = sum(y * y for y in b) ** 0.5
    return dot / (na * nb)

# Illustrative topic vectors -- not computed by a real encoder here.
topic_billing = [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.0]
topic_security = [0.0, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0]
topic_onboarding = [0.0, 0.0, 0.9, 0.1]

# A whole-document vector that discusses all three topics, pooled together.
whole_doc_vector = [
    sum(v[i] for v in (topic_billing, topic_security, topic_onboarding)) / 3
    for i in range(4)
]

query_about_security = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]

print(round(cosine(query_about_security, whole_doc_vector), 4))  # 0.5955
print(round(cosine(query_about_security, topic_security), 4))    # 0.9939
```

A query specifically about security scores a dramatically lower similarity (0.5955) against the blurred, whole-document vector than it would against a vector representing only the security-relevant section (0.9939) -- even though the document genuinely does contain excellent, on-topic security content. The document didn't get worse; the single vector's ability to point specifically at any one of its three topics got worse, purely from trying to represent all three simultaneously in one fixed-size slot. Chunking each topic into its own piece, and embedding each piece separately, is what lets the security-relevant text get its own sharp, undiluted vector instead of one smeared across everything else in the document.

sections.heading: Silent Truncation Is a Silent Failure, Not a Degraded One
sections.body:
It's worth being precise about exactly what kind of failure truncation is, because 'a slightly less complete vector' undersells it considerably. Truncation doesn't produce a fuzzier, lower-quality representation of the *whole* document -- it produces a perfectly normal-looking vector for a *different, shorter* document: whatever happened to fit within the token limit. Everything past the cutoff isn't represented poorly; it isn't represented at all. If the answer to a future query lives in paragraph 40 of a 60-paragraph document that got truncated at paragraph 12, no amount of clever querying or reranking downstream will ever surface it, because that content was never encoded into anything a similarity search could find in the first place.

This specific failure mode is dangerous precisely because it's invisible during development: a team ingests a knowledge base, checks that search returns *some* plausible-looking results for their test queries -- which are likely to hit content near the beginning of documents, since that's what a quick manual smoke test tends to probe -- ships it, and only discovers months later, usually via a confused support ticket, that an entire category of questions about later sections of longer documents has never worked, for any document, the whole time. The fix isn't a smarter model; it's checking real document lengths against the embedding model's actual token limit during ingestion, and chunking anything that would otherwise be silently cut.

sections.heading: Chunking as a Deliberate, Offline Decision
sections.body:
Given both problems above -- the hard length limit, and the granularity problem that exists independently of it -- chunking earns its place as a first-class step in any real embedding pipeline, not an occasional workaround for unusually long documents. Critically, it happens **offline**, as part of building the index, before a single embedding call is made: take a source document, split it into a set of chunks according to some strategy (the subject of the next concept), and *then* embed each chunk independently, storing each one as its own row in the vector database, typically alongside metadata that still points back to the parent document -- its title, source path, permissions, timestamp -- exactly the metadata filtering fields from the previous module.

This has a consequence worth internalizing early: from the moment chunking happens onward, a 'document' in your search index doesn't really exist as a directly retrievable unit anymore -- only its chunks do. Retrieval, ranking, and filtering all operate at the chunk level, and it's a very common (and very fixable) design mistake to forget this and write application code that still assumes 'one document equals one search result,' when what's actually being retrieved and ranked is one chunk out of potentially dozens belonging to the same source document.

examples.title: Silent Truncation Loses Everything Past the Cutoff
examples.code:
def tokenize(text):
    return text.split()

def truncate(tokens, max_tokens):
    return tokens[:max_tokens]

def toy_embed(text, max_tokens=8):
    tokens = tokenize(text)
    truncated = truncate(tokens, max_tokens)
    seed = sum(len(t) for t in truncated)
    return [(seed % 5) / 5, (seed % 7) / 7]

document = (
    "The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent driven "
    "primarily by the new enterprise product line launched in March "
    "which exceeded internal projections"
)

print(len(tokenize(document)))
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8))
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=100))
examples.explanation: tokenize(document) shows the document is 23 tokens long, but toy_embed is called with max_tokens=8, so truncate keeps only the first 8 tokens -- "The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent" -- and the returned vector, [0.8, 0.0], is computed entirely from those 8 words. Nothing about "driven primarily by the new enterprise product line launched in March which exceeded internal projections" -- the actual news in this document -- ever reaches the seed calculation. Calling toy_embed with max_tokens=100 (enough to cover the whole 23-token document) produces a completely different vector, [0.0, 0.0], computed from the real, full content. Both calls run without error and both look like ordinary embedding vectors; nothing in the output distinguishes 'this is a faithful representation of the document' from 'this is a faithful representation of the first 8 words of the document, and nothing else.'

examples.title: One Blurred Vector vs. a Sharp, Topic-Specific One
examples.code:
def cosine(a, b):
    dot = sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
    na = sum(x * x for x in a) ** 0.5
    nb = sum(y * y for y in b) ** 0.5
    return dot / (na * nb)

topic_billing = [0.9, 0.1, 0.0, 0.0]
topic_security = [0.0, 0.9, 0.1, 0.0]
topic_onboarding = [0.0, 0.0, 0.9, 0.1]

whole_doc_vector = [
    sum(v[i] for v in (topic_billing, topic_security, topic_onboarding)) / 3
    for i in range(4)
]

query_about_security = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]

print(round(cosine(query_about_security, whole_doc_vector), 4))
print(round(cosine(query_about_security, topic_security), 4))
examples.explanation: whole_doc_vector averages the three illustrative topic vectors coordinate-by-coordinate, standing in for what a real encoder's pooling step would do to a document that discusses billing, security, and onboarding all in one place. Against a query about security, that blurred vector scores only 0.5955 -- noticeably lower than the 0.9939 it would score if the security content had been embedded on its own, as its own chunk. Nothing about the underlying security content changed between the two comparisons; the only difference is whether that content had to share one vector with two unrelated topics or got a vector entirely to itself. This is the granularity problem in miniature, and it is completely independent of any token limit -- it would happen even for a hypothetical embedding model with no length restriction at all.

misconceptions.description: As long as the generation LLM has a huge context window (128k tokens or more), you don't need to chunk documents for RAG at all -- just embed and retrieve whole documents.
misconceptions.clarification: The generation model's context window and the embedding model's context window are two independent limits enforced by two different models. A generation model accepting 128k tokens says nothing about how many tokens the separate embedding model -- the one that has to turn each document into a searchable vector in the first place -- can accept before it starts silently truncating. And even for a hypothetical embedding model with no length limit whatsoever, the retrieval-granularity problem still applies: one vector representing an entire multi-topic document is a blurrier, less discriminating representation of any single one of its topics than a vector built from that topic alone would be. Chunking addresses both problems; solving the generation model's context window addresses neither.

misconceptions.description: If a document is too long for the embedding model, truncating it just gives you a slightly less complete, slightly lower-quality vector -- still roughly representative of the whole document.
misconceptions.clarification: Truncation doesn't degrade the vector's fidelity to the whole document -- it produces a vector for a different, shorter document: whatever text happened to fall before the cutoff. Content past that point isn't represented approximately; it isn't represented at all, and no later step (reranking, filtering, or anything else) can recover information that was never encoded into a vector to begin with. This is precisely why the failure is dangerous: the resulting vector looks completely ordinary, and nothing about it signals that a large fraction of the source document was silently discarded before the embedding call ever ran.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and what does the difference between the two toy_embed calls demonstrate about truncation?
exercises.code:
def tokenize(text):
    return text.split()

def truncate(tokens, max_tokens):
    return tokens[:max_tokens]

def toy_embed(text, max_tokens=8):
    tokens = tokenize(text)
    truncated = truncate(tokens, max_tokens)
    seed = sum(len(t) for t in truncated)
    return [(seed % 5) / 5, (seed % 7) / 7]

document = (
    "The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent driven "
    "primarily by the new enterprise product line launched in March "
    "which exceeded internal projections"
)

print(len(tokenize(document)))
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8))
print(toy_embed(document, max_tokens=100))
hints: tokenize just splits on whitespace -- count the words in the document string to get the first printed number.
toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8) only ever looks at the first 8 words. Compute seed as the sum of the lengths of exactly those 8 words: 'The quarterly report shows revenue grew fourteen percent'.
The document only has 23 words total, so max_tokens=100 doesn't change anything about which words get used -- truncate(tokens, 100) just returns the full 23-word list unchanged.
exercises.solutionExplanation: tokenize(document).split() produces 23 words, so the first print is 23. For toy_embed(document, max_tokens=8), truncate keeps only the first 8 words -- 'The', 'quarterly', 'report', 'shows', 'revenue', 'grew', 'fourteen', 'percent' -- whose lengths sum to 49; 49 % 5 = 4 so the first coordinate is 4/5 = 0.8, and 49 % 7 = 0 so the second coordinate is 0/7 = 0.0, giving [0.8, 0.0]. For toy_embed(document, max_tokens=100), truncate(tokens, 100) returns all 23 words unchanged since the document is shorter than the limit; summing the lengths of all 23 words happens to produce a seed that is an exact multiple of both 5 and 7, giving [0.0, 0.0]. The key takeaway isn't the exact numbers -- it's that the two calls, one truncated and one not, silently produce two completely different vectors from the same input string, with nothing in either result indicating which one actually saw the whole document.

exercises.prompt: A knowledge-base search feature embeds each document directly with this ingestion function. After launch, users report that questions about anything mentioned after the first sentence or two of a longer document never return that document, no matter how they phrase the question. Find the bug and fix it.
hints: toy_embed has a default max_tokens=8, and ingest_document never passes anything else -- how many words of `document` actually reach the seed calculation?
Count how many words in `document` come before and after that 8-word cutoff. Is the sentence about director sign-off anywhere within the first 8 words?

The fix isn't a bigger max_tokens (that only pushes the same problem further out for even longer documents) -- it's splitting `document` into pieces that each fit within the limit, and embedding and storing every piece, not just the first one.
exercises.solutionExplanation: ingest_document calls toy_embed(text) with no max_tokens argument, so it silently falls back to the default of 8 -- and toy_embed itself only ever looks at tokens[:max_tokens], discarding everything else with no warning. The director-sign-off sentence, which is what users are actually asking about, sits well past word 8 of this document, so it was never part of the seed calculation for the single vector stored under "policy-1" -- the stored vector represents only 'Vacation requests are reviewed by the team lead.' and nothing else, no matter how the document actually reads. The fix adds chunk_by_tokens, which splits the full token list into consecutive groups of at most max_tokens words, and has ingest_document embed and store every one of those groups under its own key, instead of handing the whole document to toy_embed and letting it quietly truncate. Now the sign-off sentence lives inside its own chunk (whichever one it falls into) with its own vector, so a query about director sign-off has a chunk to actually match against -- increasing max_tokens would only have delayed this same bug until the next document that's a little longer still.

assessments.prompt: A team switches their RAG pipeline's generation model to one with a 200,000-token context window and concludes they no longer need to chunk documents before indexing them. What is wrong with this conclusion?
options: Nothing is wrong -- with that much context window, whole documents can be embedded and retrieved directly.

The generation model's context window has no bearing on the embedding model's own, typically much smaller, input limit, and even without any length limit at all, embedding an entire multi-topic document into one vector still dilutes that vector's ability to represent any single topic well.
Larger context windows make embedding models slower, so chunking is still needed purely for latency reasons.
Chunking is only relevant for documents in PDF format, not plain text.
assessments.explanation: The generation model and the embedding model are two separate components with two separate, independently-enforced limits -- upgrading the model that reads retrieved text at the end of the pipeline says nothing about the model that turns documents into searchable vectors near the beginning of it. Beyond that hard limit, there's a second, completely independent reason chunking matters: even a hypothetical embedding model with no length limit at all would still produce a single vector that has to represent every topic in a long document simultaneously, diluting its similarity to a query about any one specific topic. Option A is the flawed conclusion the question is testing for. Option C invents a latency mechanism that isn't the actual reason chunking matters here. Option D is a fabricated, format-based distinction -- chunking is about token/content length and topical breadth, not file type.

assessments.prompt: A document gets silently truncated by an embedding model's token limit before being embedded. Which statement best describes what happened to the resulting vector?
options: The vector still represents the whole document, just with slightly reduced fidelity for content near the end.

The vector represents an entirely different, shorter document -- whatever text happened to fall before the cutoff -- and content past that point isn't represented approximately, it isn't represented at all.
The vector will contain a special marker value flagging that truncation occurred, which downstream code can check for and handle.
The vector's dimensionality is automatically reduced to reflect the shorter effective input, making it incompatible with un-truncated vectors stored in the same index.
assessments.explanation: The explanation is explicit that truncation is a silent failure, not a degraded one: it doesn't produce a fuzzier representation of the whole document, it produces a completely ordinary-looking vector for a different, shorter document -- whatever text happened to fit within the limit. Option A understates the failure as mere reduced fidelity, when the truth is starker: content past the cutoff is never seen by the model at all. Option C is fabricated -- nothing about a standard embedding call flags truncation in its output; that's precisely why the failure is dangerous. Option D is also fabricated -- a model's fixed output dimensionality doesn't change based on how much of the input was actually used; a truncated and non-truncated call from the same model produce vectors of identical dimensionality, just computed from different underlying text.

assessments.prompt: After a team introduces chunking into their pipeline, their application code still displays results as if each one corresponds to exactly one whole source document. What design mistake does this reflect?
options: There is no mistake -- chunking has no effect on what a single search result actually represents.

Once chunking happens, retrieval, ranking, and filtering all operate at the chunk level -- a search result is one chunk out of potentially dozens belonging to the same source document, not the document as a whole -- and code built around 'one document equals one result' no longer matches reality.
The mistake is purely cosmetic and has no bearing on which content actually gets embedded, searched, or ranked.
This pattern indicates the embedding model was never actually given any chunked text, and is still embedding whole documents.
assessments.explanation: The explanation calls this out directly as a common, fixable design mistake: from the moment chunking happens, a 'document' doesn't exist as a directly retrievable unit in the index anymore -- only its chunks do, each stored and ranked independently, typically alongside metadata pointing back to the parent document. Option A denies a consequence the explanation states outright. Option C wrongly treats a structural mismatch between what's retrieved (chunks) and what the UI assumes (whole documents) as having no functional impact, when it can directly affect how results are grouped, deduplicated, or displayed to a user. Option D is an unrelated, unsupported inference -- the mistake described is about downstream application code's assumptions, not about whether ingestion actually chunked the text.

assessments.prompt: In the worked example, a document discussing billing, security, and onboarding roughly equally produces one pooled vector. A query about security scores only 0.5955 against that whole-document vector, but 0.9939 against a vector built from the security content alone. What causes this gap?
options: The whole-document vector is mathematically incorrect, reflecting a bug in how the pooling step was implemented.

Averaging together vectors representing three different topics pulls the resulting vector toward the geometric middle of all three, making it less closely aligned with any single one of them than a vector built from just that one topic would be.
The gap only appears because cosine similarity happens to be the metric used here; a different distance metric would show no meaningful difference between the two comparisons.
The security-related content in the document must be lower quality or less detailed than the billing and onboarding content.
assessments.explanation: The whole-document vector is literally computed as the coordinate-wise average of the three topic vectors, so geometrically it sits roughly in the middle of all three -- closer to each one than a totally unrelated vector would be, but measurably less aligned with any single one than a vector built purely from that topic. That dilution, not a bug, is exactly the mechanism the example is demonstrating, ruling out option A. Option C is wrong -- the dilution effect comes from how the vector itself was constructed (averaging), not from which similarity formula is used to measure it afterward; a different metric would still show a gap, just possibly a different-looking number. Option D introduces an assumption about content quality that has nothing to do with the actual mechanism at play, which is purely geometric.

assessments.prompt: A colleague setting up their first RAG pipeline says: 'Our generation model supports a 128k-token context window, so I'm just going to embed and retrieve whole documents instead of dealing with chunking.' Explain what you'd tell them.
assessments.modelAnswer: I'd point out that this plan runs into two separate problems, and the 128k-token generation context window doesn't touch either of them. First, the embedding model used to build the searchable index is a completely different component from the generation model, with its own input limit -- commonly a few hundred to a few thousand tokens, nowhere near 128k -- and many embedding libraries handle an over-length input by silently truncating it: keeping the first N tokens and discarding the rest with no error and no warning. Anything past that cutoff is not embedded at all, so a question about content from later in a long document would never find that document in search results, no matter how large the generation model's own context window is, because the relevant content was never encoded into a retrievable vector in the first place. Second, and this is the part that would still matter even for a hypothetical embedding model with an unlimited input length: a single vector has to represent everything a document discusses simultaneously, and if that document covers several distinct subtopics, the resulting vector ends up as a blurred average across all of them -- closer to each individual topic than a totally unrelated vector would be, but noticeably less close than a vector built from just that one topic's content would be. A query about one specific subtopic of a long, multi-topic document would score a mediocre similarity against that document's single blurred vector, even though the document genuinely contains a great answer to that query somewhere inside it. Chunking solves both problems at once: splitting the document into smaller pieces before embedding keeps each piece safely under the embedding model's own limit, and gives each subtopic its own sharp, undiluted vector instead of one shared, blurred vector for the whole document. The generation model's large context window is still useful -- it's why you can retrieve and hand over several chunks at once instead of just one -- but it solves a different problem than either of these.

concepts.title: Fixed-Size, Recursive, and Semantic Chunking
concepts.description: Once you've accepted that documents must be split into chunks, the real design question is how -- naive fixed-size splitting is fast but blind to sentence and paragraph structure, recursive splitting respects that structure while still enforcing a hard size ceiling, and semantic chunking goes further still, using the embeddings themselves to find where a topic actually shifts.
learningObjectives: Implement fixed-size chunking and identify its defining weakness: it cuts wherever the character or token count lands, with no regard for sentence or word boundaries.

Explain recursive chunking: splitting hierarchically along a prioritized list of separators so natural boundaries -- paragraphs, then sentences, then words -- are preferred whenever they fit the size budget.
Explain semantic chunking conceptually: detecting a chunk boundary from a drop in embedding similarity between adjacent sentences, rather than from any fixed character or token count.
Compare the computational cost, implementation complexity, and structure-awareness of all three strategies, and identify a document type suited to each.
Predict, given a piece of text and a chunk size, exactly where fixed-size chunking will cut, including mid-word and mid-fact splits.

sections.heading: Fixed-Size Chunking: Fast, Deterministic, and Blind
sections.body:
The simplest possible chunking strategy is to just cut the text every N characters (or every N tokens), full stop:

```python
def fixed_size_chunk(text, size):
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), size)]
```

This has real, legitimate advantages: it's a few lines of code with no dependencies, it's fast enough to run over an enormous corpus without a second thought, and it's completely deterministic -- the same text and size always produce the same chunks, which makes debugging and reasoning about the resulting index straightforward. None of that changes the fact that it has absolutely no concept of what a sentence, a word, or a complete thought is; it cuts wherever the count happens to land, and the count does not care what it's in the middle of.

```python
text = (
    "The vendor invoice was flagged for review because "
    "the tax identification number on file did not match "
    "government records."
)
for chunk in fixed_size_chunk(text, 50):
    print(repr(chunk))
```

Running this splits the passage into 'The vendor invoice was flagged for review because ', 'the tax identification number on file did not matc', and 'h government records.' -- notice that the *reason* the invoice was flagged (the tax ID mismatch) is separated from the fact that it *was* flagged, and the word 'match' itself gets cut in half between the second and third chunk. Neither resulting chunk, embedded and stored on its own, fully answers 'why was this invoice flagged?' -- the first says something was flagged but not why; the second gives a reason but never says what it applies to. This is not a contrived edge case -- it's the default, unavoidable behavior of cutting on a raw count, applied to completely ordinary prose.

sections.heading: Recursive Chunking: A Prioritized List of Separators
Semantic Chunking: Boundaries Discovered From Meaning, Not Position
sections.body:
Recursive chunking's separators -- blank lines, sentence punctuation, whitespace -- are still purely syntactic guesses about where a topic probably changes. For content where topic shifts don't reliably line up with any of those markers -- meeting transcripts, chat logs, stream-of-consciousness notes -- even a well-implemented recursive splitter is just following formatting conventions that may have nothing to do with where the actual subject matter changes.

**Semantic chunking** takes a fundamentally different approach: embed each individual sentence, compute the similarity between every pair of *adjacent* sentence embeddings, and treat a sharp drop in that similarity as evidence that the topic just shifted -- cut a new chunk boundary exactly there, regardless of whether that point happens to fall near a paragraph break or not.

```python
sentence_similarities = [0.95, 0.92, 0.40, 0.90, 0.93, 0.35, 0.88]
# similarity between sentence i and sentence i+1, for 8 sentences

def find_boundaries(sims, threshold):
    return [i + 1 for i, s in enumerate(sims) if s < threshold]

print(find_boundaries(sentence_similarities, threshold=0.6))  # [3, 6]
```

Two sharp similarity drops -- between sentences 3 and 4, and between sentences 6 and 7 -- mark two genuine topic shifts, splitting these 8 sentences into three semantically coherent groups: sentences 1-3, 4-6, and 7-8. This costs real, additional compute: it requires embedding every individual sentence as its own preprocessing pass, before the 'real' chunk-level embeddings ever get computed, on top of whatever the eventual chunk embeddings will cost -- a materially more expensive pipeline than either fixed-size or recursive chunking, both of which require zero model calls to decide where to cut.

sections.heading: Choosing Among the Three
sections.body:
None of these three strategies is a universally 'best' choice -- they trade cost and structure-awareness against each other, and the right default depends on the content. Fixed-size chunking is a reasonable quick option only for short-form, largely homogeneous text where an occasional bad cut is low-stakes, or as a rapid prototype before investing in anything more careful. Recursive chunking is the sane default for most real production pipelines: it costs nothing beyond ordinary string operations, and for the large majority of well-formatted documents -- Markdown, docs with clear headings, prose with real paragraph breaks -- respecting that existing structure captures most of the practical benefit semantic chunking would otherwise provide, at a tiny fraction of the cost. Semantic chunking earns its extra expense specifically when topic shifts are frequent and genuinely don't align with any syntactic marker in the source text at all.

A common, costly mistake worth flagging explicitly: running fixed-size or naive recursive chunking over structured technical content -- Markdown with code fences, or source code itself -- without including a structure-specific separator (like a code-fence delimiter, or a function or class boundary) as a high-priority entry in the separator list. Splitting purely on paragraph breaks or raw character counts can cut a code block cleanly in half, embedding a fragment that isn't even syntactically valid on its own and that means nothing out of context -- a chunking mistake that's much easier to prevent upfront than to notice after the fact, since the resulting chunk still embeds and stores without any error.

examples.title: Fixed-Size Chunking Cuts the Reason Away From the Fact
examples.explanation: The three resulting chunks are 'The vendor invoice was flagged for review because ', 'the tax identification number on file did not matc', and 'h government records.'. The word 'match' is split into 'matc' and 'h' across the chunk boundary, but the more damaging split is semantic, not just literal: the first chunk states that an invoice was flagged, and the second chunk states a reason (a tax ID mismatch), but neither chunk alone connects the two -- a query asking 'why was the invoice flagged?' would need both chunks to fully answer, and a search system that only retrieves the single best-matching chunk (the normal case) would very plausibly surface only one half of the story.

examples.title: Recursive Chunking Falls Back to Whole-Word Boundaries
examples.explanation: The first two paragraphs (23 and 46 characters) are well under the 60-character budget, so each survives as a single, complete, untouched chunk -- exactly its own natural paragraph. The third paragraph is far too long to survive the paragraph-level split intact, so recursive_chunk recurses into it: there's no '. ' inside it (it's grammatically one long sentence), so it falls through to splitting on spaces, producing three word-boundary-respecting pieces of length 60, 58, and 24. Every single cut in the whole result lands between two complete words -- never inside one -- which is exactly the guarantee fixed-size chunking cannot offer.

examples.title: Finding Topic Boundaries From a Drop in Similarity
examples.code:
sentence_similarities = [0.95, 0.92, 0.40, 0.90, 0.93, 0.35, 0.88]

def find_boundaries(sims, threshold):
    return [i + 1 for i, s in enumerate(sims) if s < threshold]

print(find_boundaries(sentence_similarities, threshold=0.6))
examples.explanation: sentence_similarities[i] represents the similarity between sentence i+1 and sentence i+2 in a hypothetical eight-sentence passage. Two values -- 0.40 (between sentences 3 and 4) and 0.35 (between sentences 6 and 7) -- fall well below the 0.6 threshold, so find_boundaries reports [3, 6]: cut a new chunk boundary right after sentence 3, and another right after sentence 6. Every other adjacent pair stays above 0.88, indicating the topic is continuing smoothly there. The resulting three chunks -- sentences 1-3, 4-6, and 7-8 -- were discovered purely from where the content's own meaning shifted, with no paragraph break, punctuation mark, or fixed size ever consulted.

misconceptions.description: Recursive chunking's list of separators makes it just as 'smart' or meaning-aware as semantic chunking -- they're both sophisticated alternatives to naive fixed-size chunking.
misconceptions.clarification: Recursive chunking is structure-aware, not meaning-aware: every separator in its list -- a blank line, a period and space, a plain space -- is a fixed, purely syntactic marker, chosen in advance without ever looking at what the text actually means. It works well specifically because syntactic structure (paragraphs, sentences) usually correlates with meaningful structure in well-formatted writing -- but that correlation is a convenient coincidence for typical prose, not something recursive chunking measures or verifies. Semantic chunking is the one that directly measures meaning, via embedding similarity between adjacent sentences, and it's the only one of the two that would still find the real topic boundary in text where paragraph breaks and topic shifts don't line up.

misconceptions.description: Since semantic chunking uses embeddings to decide where to cut, it always produces meaningfully better retrieval than fixed-size or recursive chunking, so it's worth using everywhere.
misconceptions.clarification: Semantic chunking's extra cost -- an embedding call per sentence, as a dedicated preprocessing pass, on top of the eventual chunk-level embeddings -- has to be worth it for a given corpus, and for a large share of well-structured real documents (technical docs, articles, anything with real paragraph breaks and clear headings), recursive chunking on structure alone already captures most of the same benefit, since syntactic and topical boundaries mostly coincide there anyway. Semantic chunking's advantage is sharpest specifically for content where that coincidence breaks down -- unstructured transcripts, chat logs, stream-of-consciousness notes -- and paying its extra cost on content that doesn't have this problem buys very little over the much cheaper recursive approach.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and which specific word ends up split across a chunk boundary?
hints: fixed_size_chunk just slices the string every 50 characters, with no awareness of where words begin or end -- count characters, not words, to find each cut point.
The first chunk is text[0:50], the second is text[50:100], and so on -- write out the string and mark the 50th and 100th character positions.
Once you have the three chunk strings, look at where the second one ends and the third one begins -- is there a complete word straddling that specific boundary?
exercises.expectedAnswer: 'The vendor invoice was flagged for review because ', then 'the tax identification number on file did not matc', then 'h government records.' -- the word 'match' is split into 'matc' and 'h'.
exercises.solutionExplanation: text[0:50] captures exactly 'The vendor invoice was flagged for review because ' (including the trailing space, since the cut is purely by character count). text[50:100] continues from character 50 through 'the tax identification number on file did not matc' -- stopping one character short of finishing the word 'match'. text[100:150] (shorter than 50 characters, since the string ends there) picks up with the single leftover letter 'h', followed by ' government records.'. Nothing about fixed_size_chunk looks at word boundaries at all -- it was pure luck that the first cut happened to land on a space rather than mid-word; the second cut landing mid-word, splitting 'match' into 'matc' and 'h', is the far more typical outcome of counting characters with no regard for what they spell.

exercises.prompt: Implement `recursive_chunk(text, max_size, separators)`: try splitting `text` on `separators[0]` first; if that produces only one piece (the separator never appears), recurse with `separators[1:]` on the whole text. Otherwise, greedily reassemble the pieces into chunks that each stay within `max_size`, recursing into any single piece that is itself still too long. Then chunk the sample document with separators ["\n\n", ". ", " "] and max_size=60.
exercises.code:
def split_on(text, sep):
    return [p for p in text.split(sep) if p]

def recursive_chunk(text, max_size, separators):
    # TODO: implement as described in the prompt.
    pass

doc = (
    "Paragraph one is short.\n\n"
    "Paragraph two is also fairly short and simple.\n\n"
    "Paragraph three is much longer and goes on for quite a while "
    "describing many details that would not normally fit into a "
    "small chunk size at all."
)
for chunk in recursive_chunk(doc, 60, ["\n\n", ". ", " "]):
    print(len(chunk), repr(chunk))
hints: Base case: if len(text) <= max_size, or there are no separators left to try, just return [text] -- nothing left to split.
Split on separators[0]. If that gives back only one piece, the separator didn't appear anywhere in this text, so recurse immediately with separators[1:] instead.

Otherwise, walk the pieces and greedily glue them back together (re-inserting the separator between them) into a running `current` chunk, flushing `current` into the results list whenever adding the next piece would exceed max_size -- and recursing into any individual piece that's still too long on its own, using the remaining separators.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Splitting doc on "\n\n" first produces three pieces -- the three paragraphs -- so the function proceeds to the greedy reassembly loop rather than recursing immediately. The first two paragraphs (23 and 46 characters) each fit under 60 characters on their own and get flushed as complete chunks. The third paragraph is over 150 characters, far too long to fit -- so instead of being force-cut at 60 characters, it gets passed to recursive_chunk again with the remaining separators [". ", " "]; there's no ". " inside it, so that recursion falls through immediately to splitting on " ", which greedily reassembles individual words into three chunks of length 60, 58, and 24, none of which cut through the middle of a word. The final result has five chunks total: two whole paragraphs plus three word-respecting pieces of the third, oversized paragraph.

assessments.prompt: What is the key difference between recursive chunking and semantic chunking?
options: Recursive chunking is only for code, and semantic chunking is only for prose.

Recursive chunking splits on a prioritized list of fixed, syntactic separators (paragraph breaks, then sentences, then words); semantic chunking measures embedding similarity between adjacent sentences and cuts wherever that similarity drops, regardless of syntax.
They are two names for the same algorithm, differing only in implementation language.
Recursive chunking requires a trained embedding model; semantic chunking does not.
assessments.explanation: Recursive chunking never looks at meaning at all -- it works purely off of fixed, predetermined syntactic markers, falling back down its separator list only when a higher-priority one doesn't produce small-enough pieces. Semantic chunking's entire mechanism is different: it embeds individual sentences and cuts based on where the *meaning* actually shifts, which can happen anywhere, independent of any paragraph or sentence boundary. Option A invents a content-type restriction that doesn't exist for either strategy. Option C is wrong -- they produce different chunk boundaries on the same input whenever syntactic and semantic structure diverge. Option D has the dependency exactly backwards: semantic chunking is the one that requires an embedding model (to measure sentence-to-sentence similarity); recursive chunking needs nothing but ordinary string splitting.

assessments.prompt: Despite being blind to sentence and word boundaries, fixed-size chunking has some genuine, legitimate advantages according to the explanation. Which of the following is one of them?
options: It always produces chunks that are more semantically coherent than recursive chunking would produce on the same text.
It requires no dependencies, runs fast enough over an enormous corpus without a second thought, and is fully deterministic -- the same text and size always produce exactly the same chunks.
It automatically detects and avoids cutting through Markdown code blocks or other structured content.
It improves its cut points over time by training a small classifier on which boundaries produced better retrieval results.
assessments.explanation: The explanation is explicit about fixed-size chunking's real advantages: it's a few lines of code with no dependencies, fast enough for an enormous corpus, and completely deterministic, which makes debugging and reasoning about the resulting index straightforward. Option A is false -- fixed-size chunking is specifically the LEAST structure-aware of the three strategies, not the most coherent. Option C describes exactly the kind of failure the explanation warns fixed-size (and naive recursive) chunking is prone to when applied to technical content, not something it avoids automatically. Option D describes a learning mechanism fixed-size chunking doesn't have at all -- it applies the exact same fixed rule (cut every N characters) regardless of any feedback.

assessments.prompt: In recursive chunking, suppose splitting a document on the highest-priority separator (a blank line between paragraphs) leaves one resulting paragraph still too large for the size budget. What happens next?
options: That oversized paragraph is force-cut at the exact character limit, regardless of word boundaries -- the same behavior fixed-size chunking would produce.
The entire document is discarded and re-processed from scratch using only whitespace splitting.

That specific oversized paragraph is recursively split again using the next separator down the prioritized list (such as sentence-ending punctuation, then plain whitespace), continuing to respect structure rather than falling back to an arbitrary character cut.
The oversized paragraph is embedded exactly as-is, exceeding the size budget, since recursive chunking has no hard ceiling on chunk size.
assessments.explanation: This is the core mechanism of recursive chunking: only the specific piece that's still too large gets recursed into, using the remaining, lower-priority separators in order -- sentence punctuation next, then plain whitespace as a last resort -- so structure is respected as much as possible before ever falling back to a less natural boundary. Option A describes fixed-size chunking's behavior, which is exactly what recursive chunking is designed to avoid until every other separator has been exhausted. Option B invents a wasteful, all-or-nothing restart that isn't how the algorithm works -- only the oversized piece recurses, not the whole document. Option D is wrong -- the whole point of the recursion is to keep chunks within the size budget; recursive chunking does enforce a hard ceiling, it just tries harder than fixed-size chunking to respect structure while doing so.

assessments.prompt: Why does semantic chunking require materially more compute than either fixed-size or recursive chunking?
options: It requires embedding every individual sentence as a dedicated preprocessing pass, on top of whatever chunk-level embeddings eventually get computed -- whereas neither fixed-size nor recursive chunking requires any model calls at all to decide where to cut.
It requires re-embedding the entire corpus multiple times in a loop until the detected boundaries stop changing.
It only works with the largest and most expensive embedding models available, unlike fixed-size or recursive chunking, which can use any model.
It requires running the generation LLM once for every candidate boundary to judge whether a topic shift actually occurred there.
assessments.explanation: Semantic chunking's defining extra cost is exactly this: it embeds every sentence individually to compute adjacent-sentence similarity, as a separate pass that happens before the chunk-level embeddings are ever computed -- fixed-size and recursive chunking both decide where to cut using zero model calls, which is precisely why they're so much cheaper. Option B invents an iterative re-embedding loop that isn't part of the described mechanism at all -- boundaries are determined from one pass of adjacent-sentence similarities, not from repeated re-embedding. Option C is a fabricated constraint -- semantic chunking's sentence-level embeddings could in principle use any embedding model, small or large. Option D confuses semantic chunking's actual mechanism (embedding similarity) with the generation LLM, which plays no role in deciding chunk boundaries at all.

assessments.prompt: A teammate is about to run naive fixed-size chunking over a corpus of technical documentation that includes Markdown code blocks. Explain what could go wrong, and what you'd recommend instead.
assessments.modelAnswer: Fixed-size chunking cuts on a raw character or token count with absolutely no awareness of what it's cutting through, and a Markdown code block is exactly the kind of content where that's most damaging: a fixed-size cut can land in the middle of a function definition, splitting it across two chunks, each of which is now a syntactically broken code fragment that means very little on its own and would embed into a vector representing, at best, a confusing partial snippet rather than the actual, complete function it came from. Worse, this happens completely silently -- the chunking code runs without error, the resulting fragment still gets embedded and stored just like any other chunk, and there's no signal anywhere that a code block was severed until someone notices retrieval quality is oddly poor for code-related queries specifically. I'd recommend switching to recursive chunking with a separator list that treats code-fence boundaries (triple backticks) as a high-priority separator, ahead of generic paragraph or sentence splitting -- so that, wherever possible, an entire code block stays intact as its own chunk (or stays grouped with the prose immediately around it) rather than being split at an arbitrary character count that has no idea it's inside a fenced block. If individual functions or code blocks are still too large even after that, a further split on function or class boundaries -- rather than raw line count -- keeps each resulting piece syntactically meaningful on its own, which matters a lot for how well it can be embedded and matched against a query in the first place.

concepts.title: Chunk Size, Overlap, and the Precision/Context Tradeoff
concepts.description: Chunk size and overlap are the two knobs that actually control how well retrieval works in practice -- a chunk too small severs a fact from the context it needs to make sense, a chunk too large dilutes relevance the same way an entire undivided document does, and overlap mitigates boundary damage without ever fully eliminating it, at a real, measurable storage and latency cost.
learningObjectives: Explain the two-sided failure mode of chunk size: chunks too small losing necessary surrounding context, versus chunks too large diluting relevance, and connect the 'too large' case back to the granularity problem.
Explain what overlap is mechanically, and how it increases the chance that a fact sitting near a chunk boundary ends up whole in at least one stored chunk.
Compute how the number of chunks -- and therefore embedding and storage cost -- produced from a fixed-length document changes as overlap increases, for a fixed chunk size.
Describe an evidence-based process for choosing chunk size and overlap for a real corpus, rather than adopting a library's default values unexamined.
Diagnose, given a specific retrieval failure, whether it is better explained by chunk size being too large, too small, or by insufficient overlap.

sections.heading: Two Failure Modes on the Same Knob
sections.body:
Chunk size sits on a single numeric axis, but it fails in two entirely different directions, and it's worth being explicit that 'smaller is safer' is not a rule you can lean on. A chunk that's **too small** can sever a fact from the context that gives it meaning: a table row without its header row, a sentence like 'the request was ultimately denied' without whatever preceded it that says which request, or a single clause of a larger conditional statement with the condition itself sitting in the previous, unretrieved chunk. A chunk that's small enough to be sharply on-topic can still be useless if it's too small to be *self-contained*.

A chunk that's **too large** runs into the granularity problem from the first concept in this module, just at a smaller scale than a whole undivided document: the more distinct ideas a single chunk covers, the more its one pooled vector has to represent all of them simultaneously, and the less sharply it represents any one of them. A chunk covering five loosely related paragraphs is, in miniature, exactly the same problem as embedding an entire 50-page document as one vector -- just with slightly fewer topics diluting the result. Neither failure mode announces itself with an error; both just produce retrieval that's quietly worse than it should be, for reasons that only become clear once you go looking at exactly what got retrieved and exactly what it was missing.

sections.heading: What Overlap Actually Buys You
sections.body:
**Overlap** means each chunk after the first repeats the tail end of the chunk before it, rather than starting exactly where the previous one left off:

```python
def chunk_with_overlap(text, size, overlap):
    step = size - overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]
```

Instead of advancing by the full `size` on every chunk, the window only advances by `size - overlap`, so the last `overlap` characters of one chunk reappear as the first `overlap` characters of the next. The point of doing this is to rescue facts that would otherwise land squarely on a chunk boundary and get cut in half:

```python
text = (
    "Refunds are approved only when the return request is "
    "submitted within 30 days of the delivery date, no exceptions."
)

no_overlap = chunk_with_overlap(text, size=75, overlap=0)
with_overlap = chunk_with_overlap(text, size=75, overlap=20)

print(any("30 days" in c for c in no_overlap))    # False
print(any("30 days" in c for c in with_overlap))  # True
```

With no overlap, a 75-character chunk size happens to cut right through the middle of '30 days' -- 'within 30 da' ends one chunk, 'ys of the delivery date...' begins the next, and the crucial number-plus-unit never appears whole in either one. With a 20-character overlap, the second chunk starts 20 characters earlier than it otherwise would -- early enough to fully re-include '30 days' along with context on both sides, inside that one chunk, even though the *first* chunk still ends at the exact same awkward spot as before. Overlap doesn't fix every individual boundary; it adds an additional, shifted chunk that has a real chance of containing whole whatever the unshifted boundary happened to cut through.

sections.heading: Overlap's Real Cost: More Chunks, More Storage, More Redundant Retrieval
sections.body:
Overlap is not free, and the cost is mechanical and easy to compute ahead of time. For a document of length `L`, chunk size `S`, and overlap `O`, the window advances by `S - O` characters per step, so the total number of chunks produced is roughly `L / (S - O)`:

```python
import math

def chunk_count(length, size, overlap):
    step = size - overlap
    return math.ceil(max(length - overlap, 0) / step) if length > 0 else 0

for overlap in (0, 50, 100):
    print(overlap, chunk_count(1000, 200, overlap))

# 0   5
# 50  7
# 100 9
```

For a fixed 1,000-character document and a fixed 200-character chunk size, moving from no overlap to a 100-character overlap (half the chunk size) nearly doubles the number of chunks, from 5 to 9. Every one of those extra chunks is a separate embedding to compute at ingestion time, a separate row to store, and a separate candidate that can show up in a future top-k search result -- meaning a query's retrieved results are now more likely to include two or three heavily overlapping chunks that repeat much of the same text, rather than three or four genuinely distinct pieces of information. That's a real cost against the generation LLM's limited context budget: tokens spent on near-duplicate text are tokens not spent on additional distinct, useful content.

sections.heading: Choosing Values by Measurement, Not by Habit
sections.body:
There's no universal correct chunk size or overlap, for the same reason there's no universal correct `nprobe` or `ef_search` from the ANN indexing module: the right value depends on your actual documents and your actual queries, not on a number that worked well for someone else's corpus. The reliable process mirrors that same recall-tuning methodology: assemble a set of real (or realistically representative) questions together with the exact source text that should answer each one, then, for several candidate chunk_size/overlap settings, check whether that exact source span ends up fully contained within a single retrieved chunk -- and ultimately, check end-task answer accuracy in the full RAG pipeline, not just whether a human skimming the chunks judges them to 'look reasonable.'

A chunk size in the low hundreds of tokens, with an overlap somewhere around 10-20% of that size, is a common, reasonable place to *start* this process for general prose -- not a value to adopt permanently without checking it against your own data. A corpus of dense legal contracts, a corpus of short chat messages, and a corpus of long-form articles are different enough in their internal structure that a single chunk_size/overlap setting tuned for one of them is not a safe assumption to carry over to another, even within the same overall product.

sections.heading: Common Mistakes
sections.body: A few mistakes show up often enough to call out directly. Treating 'bigger chunks' as strictly safer, on the theory that more context can only help, ignores the granularity-dilution problem entirely -- past a certain size, a bigger chunk actively hurts the precision of retrieval, not just its cost. Using zero overlap by default, simply because it's the parameter's most obvious value, then being surprised when an important fact turns out to be split across exactly the wrong boundary -- overlap is a deliberate, worthwhile mitigation, not an optional nicety. And assuming one chunk_size/overlap setting, once chosen, applies uniformly across a corpus that actually contains structurally very different document types, when a setting well-suited to long, dense prose may be badly mismatched to short, choppy content elsewhere in the very same index.

examples.title: Overlap Rescues a Fact That a Bare Boundary Would Have Split
examples.explanation: With overlap=0, the two resulting chunks are 'Refunds are approved only when the return request is submitted within 30 da' and 'ys of the delivery date, no exceptions.' -- the number-plus-unit '30 days' is split into 'da' and 'ys' across the boundary, so neither chunk contains it whole; a query specifically about the return window would find no chunk with the complete phrase to match against. With overlap=20, the first chunk is identical (it still ends exactly where it did before), but the second chunk now starts 20 characters earlier, at 'bmitted within 30 days of the delivery date, no exceptions.' -- which does contain '30 days' whole, along with context on both sides. The fact was rescued not by fixing the original boundary, but by adding a second, shifted chunk that never hit that same boundary in the first place.

examples.title: Overlap's Cost: Chunk Count Grows as Overlap Grows
examples.explanation: For a fixed 1,000-character document and a fixed 200-character chunk size, chunk_count climbs from 5 chunks with no overlap, to 7 with a 50-character overlap, to 9 with a 100-character overlap (half the chunk size) -- nearly double the original count. Every one of those extra 4 chunks needs its own embedding computed and stored, and, more subtly, several of them now substantially repeat text that a neighboring chunk also contains -- so a top-k retrieval for this document is more likely to surface two or three chunks that are mostly the same text, crowding out chunks that would have added genuinely new information to the retrieved context.

misconceptions.description: Bigger chunks are strictly safer than smaller ones, since they include more surrounding context and can only help retrieval, never hurt it.
misconceptions.clarification: Past a certain point, a bigger chunk actively hurts retrieval precision, for exactly the same reason an entire undivided document does: the more distinct ideas packed into one chunk, the more its single pooled vector has to represent all of them at once, diluting how sharply it represents any one of them. A query about one specific idea inside an overly large chunk scores a noticeably lower similarity than it would against a smaller, more tightly-focused chunk covering just that idea -- so 'more context per chunk' trades away retrieval precision, it doesn't purely add safety margin.

misconceptions.description: Adding overlap between chunks eliminates the risk of an important fact being split across a chunk boundary.
misconceptions.clarification: Overlap reduces, but does not eliminate, that risk -- it works by adding extra, shifted chunks that have a good chance of not hitting the exact same boundary as their un-shifted neighbors, not by guaranteeing every fact stays intact everywhere. A fact longer than the overlap window, or one that happens to span more than one boundary, can still end up split even with overlap in place. Overlap is a real, worthwhile mitigation with a real, measurable storage and redundant-retrieval cost -- not a way to make chunk boundaries stop mattering.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and what does the trend across the three overlap values tell you about overlap's cost?
hints: step = size - overlap, so for overlap=0, step=200; for overlap=50, step=150; for overlap=100, step=100.
chunk_count computes math.ceil((length - overlap) / step) -- work out (1000 - overlap) / step for each of the three overlap values first.
Notice step shrinks as overlap grows, while the numerator (1000 - overlap) shrinks much more slowly -- so the ratio, and therefore the chunk count, has to grow.
exercises.solutionExplanation: For overlap=0: step=200, so chunk_count = ceil((1000-0)/200) = ceil(5.0) = 5. For overlap=50: step=150, chunk_count = ceil((1000-50)/150) = ceil(950/150) = ceil(6.33) = 7. For overlap=100: step=100, chunk_count = ceil((1000-100)/100) = ceil(900/100) = 9. As overlap grows from 0 to 100 (half the chunk size), the number of chunks needed to cover the same 1000-character document nearly doubles, from 5 to 9 -- directly, mechanically, because a bigger overlap means each chunk only advances a shorter distance past the previous one, so more of them are needed to cover the same total length. Every one of those extra chunks is an extra embedding to compute, store, and potentially retrieve alongside near-duplicate neighbors.

exercises.prompt: This chunking function is supposed to create overlapping chunks so that a fact near a boundary is likely to appear whole in at least one chunk. Instead, testing reveals it's doing the opposite -- entire stretches of the source text never appear in ANY chunk at all. Find and fix the bug.
exercises.code:
def chunk_with_overlap(text, size, overlap):
    step = size + overlap  # advance further per chunk to "add" overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]

text = "AAAAABBBBBCCCCCDDDDDEEEEEFFFFFGGGGGHHHHHIIIIIJJJJJ"
chunks = chunk_with_overlap(text, size=10, overlap=5)
for c in chunks:
    print(repr(c))
# CCCCC, FFFFF, and IIIII never appear in any chunk at all
hints: Overlap is supposed to make consecutive chunks share some trailing/leading text -- does advancing FURTHER per chunk (step = size + overlap) make chunks share more text, or less?
Work out what index each chunk starts at with step = size + overlap = 15, and compare that to where the previous chunk actually ended (start + size = start + 10). Is there a gap?
The step between chunk starts needs to be SMALLER than the chunk size for there to be any overlap at all -- that means subtracting overlap from size, not adding it.
exercises.solutionCode:
def chunk_with_overlap(text, size, overlap):
    step = size - overlap  # advance LESS than a full chunk width, to overlap
    return [text[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(text), step)]

text = "AAAAABBBBBCCCCCDDDDDEEEEEFFFFFGGGGGHHHHHIIIIIJJJJJ"
chunks = chunk_with_overlap(text, size=10, overlap=5)
for c in chunks:
    print(repr(c))
# every 5-letter group now appears in at least one chunk, several appear in two
exercises.solutionExplanation: The bug is step = size + overlap, which advances the start of each chunk FURTHER than the chunk's own width (10 + 5 = 15, but each chunk only covers 10 characters) -- creating a 5-character gap between the end of one chunk and the start of the next, rather than a 5-character overlap. That's precisely why 'CCCCC', 'FFFFF', and 'IIIII' vanish entirely: they fall exactly inside those gaps, never captured by any chunk's window at all -- a far more serious failure than a boundary merely cutting a fact in half, since this content is completely absent from the index, not just split. The fix, step = size - overlap = 5, makes each chunk start only 5 characters after the previous one began (versus a chunk width of 10), so consecutive chunks now share 5 characters of overlap instead of leaving a 5-character gap -- every letter group is captured by at least one chunk, and several are captured by two, which is the overlap behavior that was actually intended.

assessments.prompt: A team, worried about facts getting split across chunk boundaries, sets their chunk size very large -- each chunk now covers what used to be 8-10 smaller chunks. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Retrieval quality improves unconditionally, since larger chunks contain more context and are strictly safer.

Retrieval precision gets worse: each chunk's single pooled vector now has to represent many more distinct ideas at once, diluting its similarity to a query about any one specific idea -- the same granularity problem that motivated chunking whole documents in the first place, just recurring at a smaller scale.
Nothing changes, since chunk size only affects storage cost, not retrieval quality.
The embedding model will reject chunks above a certain size with an explicit error, so the team will find out immediately if this is a problem.
assessments.explanation: Chunk size increases don't just risk hitting an embedding model's hard token limit -- well before that limit, a chunk covering many distinct ideas produces a single vector that has to represent all of them simultaneously, which is a smaller-scale recurrence of exactly the whole-document granularity problem the first concept in this module covered. Option A ignores that dilution effect entirely. Option C is wrong because chunk size affects both storage cost AND retrieval precision, not just the former. Option D is wrong because many real embedding pipelines truncate silently rather than raising an explicit, catchable error -- which is precisely why the failure can go unnoticed rather than being 'found out immediately.'

assessments.prompt: A retrieved chunk contains only the sentence "The request was ultimately denied." with no surrounding text -- a reader has no way to tell which request, or why. What specific failure mode does this illustrate?
options: The chunk is too large, causing its pooled vector to dilute across too many unrelated topics.
The chunk is too small to be self-contained -- it's sharply on-topic (it really is about a denial), but severed from the context that actually gives the fact its meaning.
This specifically indicates the overlap setting was too high, causing excessive redundant retrieval.
This is evidence that the embedding model silently truncated the input before embedding it.
assessments.explanation: This is exactly the 'too small' failure mode described in the explanation: a chunk can be small enough to be sharply on-topic and still be useless because it isn't self-contained -- missing whatever preceding context (which request, what grounds) that would let the fact actually be understood on its own. Option A describes the opposite failure mode -- dilution from too many topics in one chunk, which isn't what's happening in a chunk that's arguably too narrow, not too broad. Option C misattributes the problem to overlap, which affects whether a fact gets duplicated across boundaries, not whether a single small chunk lacks context. Option D describes an unrelated failure (input exceeding a hard token limit), not the chunk-size-granularity problem this scenario is illustrating.

assessments.prompt: As overlap increases toward roughly half of the chunk size, what happens to the total number of chunks produced from a fixed-length document, and what is the direct downstream consequence?
options: The chunk count decreases, since a larger overlap means fewer distinct chunks are needed to cover the same document.

The chunk count increases substantially (potentially nearly doubling), because the window between consecutive chunk starts advances by only size-minus-overlap per step -- meaning more embeddings to compute and store, and a higher chance that a top-k retrieval surfaces several heavily redundant, overlapping chunks instead of distinct information.
The chunk count stays exactly the same regardless of overlap, since overlap changes what each chunk contains, not how many chunks there are.
The chunk count increases, but only for documents that are shorter than the configured chunk size itself.
assessments.explanation: Because the step between consecutive chunk starts is size minus overlap, a bigger overlap makes each chunk advance a shorter distance past the previous one, requiring more chunks to cover the same total document length -- the explanation's own worked numbers show chunk count nearly doubling (5 to 9) as overlap grows from 0 to half the chunk size. Each of those extra chunks is a real embedding and storage cost, and several of them substantially repeat text a neighboring chunk also contains, crowding out genuinely distinct information from a limited top-k retrieval. Option A has the relationship backwards. Option C ignores that overlap directly changes the step size and therefore the chunk count, not just chunk content. Option D invents a length-dependent exception that isn't part of how the chunk_count formula actually behaves.

assessments.prompt: A team adds a modest overlap to their chunking pipeline and concludes that important facts near a chunk boundary can no longer end up split across two chunks. Is this conclusion correct?
options: Yes -- any nonzero overlap fully guarantees that every fact stays intact within at least one chunk, no matter how long the fact is.

No -- overlap reduces this risk, by adding extra, shifted chunks that have a good chance of not hitting the exact same boundary as their un-shifted neighbors, but a fact longer than the overlap window, or one that spans more than one boundary, can still end up split even with overlap in place.
No -- overlap has no effect whatsoever on boundary-splitting risk; it only changes storage and embedding cost.
Yes, but only for chunks built from English-language text; other languages are unaffected by overlap.
assessments.explanation: The explanation states this directly as a misconception to avoid: overlap mitigates boundary damage without eliminating it, because it works by adding shifted chunks that often, but not always, avoid the exact same cut point -- a fact that's unusually long relative to the overlap window, or one spanning multiple boundaries, can still be split. Option A overclaims a guarantee the mechanism doesn't provide. Option C understates overlap's real, demonstrated benefit (rescuing '30 days' in the worked example) as having no effect at all. Option D introduces a language-specific distinction that has no basis in how overlap actually works -- the mechanism is purely about character or token position, independent of language.

assessments.prompt: A colleague building a new RAG pipeline asks how they should pick chunk_size and overlap for their specific document collection, since every blog post they've read recommends different numbers. Explain the process you'd recommend instead of picking a number from a blog post.
assessments.modelAnswer: There's no universally correct chunk_size or overlap, because the right values depend on the actual internal structure of your specific documents and the actual questions your users will ask -- exactly the same reason there's no universally correct nprobe or ef_search for an ANN index, and the right process looks similar: measure against your own data instead of adopting someone else's tuned value. Concretely, I'd start by assembling a representative set of real (or realistically written) questions, each paired with the exact span of source text that should answer it. Then, for a handful of candidate chunk_size and overlap settings, I'd check two things: first, whether that exact answer span ends up fully contained within a single chunk at each setting (a chunk size too small will often sever it, cutting away the context that makes it a complete answer); and second, and more importantly, actual end-task accuracy -- running the full retrieval-plus-generation pipeline and checking whether the final answers are actually correct, since a chunk that 'looks fine' to a human skimming it can still perform differently once it's actually competing against other chunks in a real similarity ranking. I'd start from a modest chunk size (a few hundred tokens) with overlap around 10-20% of that size purely as a reasonable starting point to tune from, not as the answer -- and I'd specifically watch for documents in the collection that are structurally very different from each other (dense legal text versus short chat messages, say), since a single setting tuned for one document type is not a safe assumption to carry over to a structurally different one, even within the same index. I'd re-run this measurement any time the corpus's document types shift meaningfully, for the same reason ANN recall tuning has to be re-checked after a data distribution shift.
